meta.title: Who really said "From so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Darwin. It is the closing sentence of On the Origin of Species (John Murray, 1859), pp. 489-90 — and “evolved” is the last word of the book.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'From so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Darwin: the final sentence of On the Origin of Species, 1859. The first edition omits “by the Creator”; editions two to six add it.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is the real thing, word for word: it is the closing sentence of On the Origin of Species (London: John Murray, 1859), the last lines of chapter XIV, “Recapitulation and Conclusion.” Wikiquote places it at pp. 489–90 of the first edition, and the 1859 text on Wikisource matches the popular wording exactly — right down to “have been, and are being, evolved.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection
Chapter XIV, “Recapitulation and Conclusion” — pp. 489–90, the closing sentence of the book
First edition text. Editions two (1860) through six (1872) insert “by the Creator” after “originally breathed.”

source.excerpt: There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.
trail: Wikisource’s transcription of the 1859 chapter XIV ↗ ends on this sentence, in the popular wording and without “by the Creator.”
Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ cites “1st ed. (1859) pp. 489–90” and notes that later editions added “by the Creator” after “originally breathed.”
The Darwin Correspondence Project ↗ quotes the sentence in full and states that it was Darwin’s first use of the word ‘evolution’, in any form, in print.

Wikipedia’s account of the book ↗ gives the first publication as 24 November 1859 by John Murray, records the “by the Creator” addition in the second edition, and notes that all editions concluded with the word “evolved.”

source.rightsNote: On the Origin of Species was first published in London by John Murray on 24 November 1859 — comfortably before the 1931 United States cutoff — and Darwin died in 1882, so both the work and this sentence are in the public domain worldwide. The text was written in English, so no translation rights are involved.

author.name: Charles Darwin
author.heading: Charles Darwin
author.metaLine: 1809–1882 · English naturalist · author of On the Origin of Species
author.bio: Charles Darwin was an English naturalist whose 1859 book On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection set out the case that species change over time through descent with modification. Published by John Murray on 24 November 1859, it went through six editions in Darwin’s lifetime, and he revised it repeatedly in response to scientific and religious objections. He was a careful, hedging writer — which is why the one soaring sentence he allowed himself, right at the end, has outlived almost everything else in the book.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: The attribution is not in doubt — this one really is Darwin. What circulates wrongly is the wording, and the phrase’s later career as a title.

items.why: Quote aggregators routinely drop the opening clause and print only “Endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being evolved” — as on Quotefancy ↗, which gives no source or edition at all. “From so simple a beginning” is the half that carries the argument.

From the second edition onward Darwin added “by the Creator”, so the 1872 sixth edition ↗ reads “originally breathed by the Creator into a few forms or into one.” Anyone quoting the famous godless version is quoting 1859 specifically.

“Endless forms most beautiful” is the title of Sean B. Carroll’s 2005 book ↗ and of Nightwish’s 2015 album ↗; both pages state the title is drawn from Darwin’s closing paragraph. The phrase is quoted, not coined, in each case.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Darwin’s own, verbatim: the closing line of On the Origin of Species, first edition, pp. 489–90 ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Darwin spent 490 pages being scrupulously careful — hedging, conceding, anticipating objections — and then, in the last sentence of the last chapter, let himself off the leash. The “entangled bank” paragraph that closes the book is the only place where he writes like a poet rather than a barnacle taxonomist, and it is the passage almost everyone can half-remember.

There is a second reason the sentence is famous. The Darwin Correspondence Project ↗ notes that this was Darwin’s first use of the word ‘evolution’, in any form, in print. Wikipedia’s account of the book adds that the sixth edition was the first in which he used the word “evolution” itself, and that all editions concluded with the word “evolved.” The word we now attach to the whole theory shows up in the founding text exactly once, as the final syllable.
context.detailsSummary: The one word Darwin changed afterwards
detailsBody: The first edition reads “having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one.” From the second edition (1860) onward, Darwin inserted “by the Creator” — so editions two through six read “originally breathed by the Creator into a few forms or into one.” Everything after that, including the phrase people quote, is unchanged.
That means a reader working from a modern paperback of the sixth edition and a reader working from the 1859 first edition will produce two slightly different closing sentences, both genuine.
context.pull: The word ‘evolution’ never appears in the 1859 book. ‘Evolved’ appears once — as the last word.
